Furthermore, for a given proposer model, the maximally permissive least-intrusive supervisor is characterized as a value-threshold refinement of the conventional one. Under precise conditions, this refinement orders two concurrent actions by at most one monitor place. On an autonomous release agent, we find by synthesis that safe deployment requires a step that the supervisor can refuse after a rollout starts.
items.title_ko: 에이전트 AI를 위한 인증된 실행 하네스: 추론과 행동 사이의 안전하고 최소 침습적인 페트리 넷 감독 제어
items.summary_ko: 이 논문은 프롬프트 주입 하에서 LLM 에이전트의 안전한 도구 실행 문제를 연구합니다. 페트리 넷을 사용하여 LLM과 도구 사이의 실행 하네스를 감독 제어 문제로 공식화하며, 마크는 기능, 승인 및 예산을 나타냅니다. 사전 조건이 충족되지 않거나 이미 소진된 주입된 요청은 내용과 관계없이 거부됩니다.
items.why_ko: LLM 에이전트의 프롬프트 주입 공격 방지 및 안전한 도구 실행 보장은 AI 시스템의 보안과 신뢰성을 강화하는 데 매우 중요합니다.

items.title: RIDAR: Safeguarding Research Integrity in Autonomous Research Agents via Automated Detection and Runtime Intervention
items.body: Autonomous research agents are increasingly used to automate large portions of scientific research, yet they are prone to research integrity violations (RIVs): behaviors that compromise the validity, reproducibility, or faithfulness of the research process. We present RIDAR, a framework for automated RIV detection and runtime intervention. First, we introduce RIVT, a comprehensive taxonomy of 14 RIV types spanning the full research lifecycle. Building on RIVT, we present RIDAR-post-hoc, a framework to detect RIVs within agent trajectories. RIDAR-post-hoc achieves 85.2% F1 performance on RIV-Gold, a benchmark for RIV detection with 60 expert-annotated trajectories. Applying RIDAR-post-hoc to RIV-Wild, a dataset of 300 agent trajectories across 50 distinct research tasks, we detect 3,964 RIV instances in 99.7% of trajectories, revealing the prevalence of RIVs in current agents. Finally, we present RIDAR-runtime, a framework for dynamically detecting and correcting RIVs during agent runtime. RIDAR-runtime effectively reduces agent RIVs remaining at task completion by 36.8%. We will release our code and data to facilitate future research.
items.title_ko: RIDAR: 자동 감지 및 런타임 개입을 통한 자율 연구 에이전트의 연구 무결성 보호
items.summary_ko: 자율 연구 에이전트는 과학 연구의 많은 부분을 자동화하는 데 점점 더 많이 사용되지만, 연구 과정의 유효성, 재현성 또는 충실도를 손상시키는 연구 무결성 위반(RIV)에 취약합니다. 이 논문은 자동 RIV 감지 및 런타임 개입을 위한 프레임워크인 RIDAR를 제시합니다.
items.why_ko: AI 기반 자율 연구 시스템의 윤리적 문제를 해결하고 연구의 무결성을 보장하는 것은 과학적 발견의 신뢰성과 AI의 책임감 있는 활용에 필수적입니다.

items.title: AfterDeleteBench: Auditing Post-Deletion Information Persistence in LLM Agents
items.body: Many LLM agents maintain external persistent memory and derive additional state from past interactions, such as summaries. Deleting an original memory record therefore need not remove information carried by its descendants. We introduce AfterDeleteBench, a controlled behavioral audit for this failure mode in fixed-weight LLM agents. For each synthetic secret, we compare an exposed-then-deleted agent with an otherwise matched agent that was never exposed to the secret, allowing post-deletion recovery to be attributed to the original exposure. In our primary setting, a single query recovers the deleted secret from Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct in roughly two thirds of cases, while matched never-exposed controls have zero recovery. Crucially, recovery does not require a surviving verbatim copy: when the complete secret string is absent and only separately stored components remain under a public composition rule, exact reconstruction succeeds in 62-99% of cases across Qwen, Mistral, and Phi-3. We also show that the response interface is part of the measurement system: target-bearing replies can be scored as failures when the requested format and parser are misaligned. Finally, we separate reconstruction from write-back and fresh-session recall. Provenance-aware closure eliminates observed recovery in the tested positive-baseline settings, whereas an exact-literal write filter blocks reinsertion but cannot erase information already present. Together, these results show that source deletion should be evaluated behaviorally at the level of the agent and its memory system, not only as a storage operation.
items.body_ko: 많은 LLM 에이전트는 외부 영구 메모리를 유지하고 요약과 같은 과거 상호 작용에서 추가 상태를 도출합니다. 따라서 원본 메모리 레코드를 삭제한다고 해서 그 파생 항목에 담긴 정보가 반드시 제거되는 것은 아닙니다. 우리는 고정 가중치 LLM 에이전트에서 이러한 오류 모드에 대한 제어된 행동 감사인 AfterDeleteBench를 소개합니다. 각 합성 비밀에 대해, 우리는 노출된 후 삭제된 에이전트와 비밀에 전혀 노출되지 않은 다른 일치하는 에이전트를 비교하여, 삭제 후 복구를 원래 노출에 귀속시킬 수 있도록 합니다. 우리의 주요 설정에서, 단일 쿼리는 Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct에서 약 3분의 2의 경우에 삭제된 비밀을 복구하는 반면, 일치하는 미노출 제어 그룹은 복구율이 0%였습니다. 결정적으로, 복구는 살아남은 원문 복사본을 필요로 하지 않습니다. 완전한 비밀 문자열이 없고 공개 구성 규칙 하에 별도로 저장된 구성 요소만 남아 있을 때, Qwen, Mistral, Phi-3에서 62-99%의 경우에 정확한 재구성이 성공합니다. 또한 우리는 응답 인터페이스가 측정 시스템의 일부임을 보여줍니다. 요청된 형식과 파서가 불일치할 때 목표를 포함하는 응답은 실패로 간주될 수 있습니다. 마지막으로, 우리는 재구성을 다시 쓰기(write-back) 및 새 세션 회상(fresh-session recall)과 분리합니다. 출처 인식 폐쇄는 테스트된 긍정 기준선 설정에서 관찰된 복구를 제거하는 반면, 정확한 리터럴 쓰기 필터는 재삽입을 차단하지만 이미 존재하는 정보를 지울 수는 없습니다. 종합적으로 이러한 결과는 소스 삭제가 저장 작업으로서만이 아니라 에이전트와 그 메모리 시스템 수준에서 행동적으로 평가되어야 함을 보여줍니다.
items.title_ko: AfterDeleteBench: LLM 에이전트에서 삭제 후 정보 지속성 감사
items.summary_ko: 많은 LLM 에이전트는 외부 영구 메모리를 유지하고 과거 상호작용에서 추가 상태(예: 요약)를 파생합니다. 따라서 원래 메모리 기록을 삭제해도 그 후손이 가지고 있는 정보가 제거되지 않을 수 있습니다. 이 논문은 고정 가중치 LLM 에이전트에서 이러한 실패 모드를 제어하여 감사하는 'AfterDeleteBench'를 소개합니다.
items.why_ko: LLM 에이전트의 '잊혀질 권리'와 데이터 삭제 후 정보 지속성 문제는 개인 정보 보호 및 규제 준수에 매우 중요하며, 이를 감사하는 벤치마크는 프라이버시 보호 기술 개발에 필수적입니다.

items.title: CrisiLangs: A Multilingual Resource for Crisis Warning Generation
items.body: Communicating with the public during an emergency entails issuing warning messages promptly. In Europe, it often requires producing them in more than one language. Recent work has shown that language models can be trained to generate warning messages as a crisis unfolds, but the available data covers only English. To fill this gap, we present CrisiLangs, a multilingual extension of CrisiText (an English dataset of crisis events paired with warning messages written according to expert communication guidelines) to Italian, Bulgarian, German, and Greek. Expert native speakers translated the warning messages of 1,000 events drawn from 411 scenarios, for a total of 5,000 event-message pairs across five languages. We test the resource to fine-tune a multilingual model on all five languages jointly, with and without the emergency guidelines in the prompt, and compare it with a zero-shot baseline. The fine-tuned models outperform the baseline on ROUGE-L, BLEU and BERTScore in every language and configuration. In a human preference study, low decoding temperatures receive the most preferences in all five languages and in both configurations, while the effect of the guidelines varies by language.
items.title_ko: CrisiLangs: 위기 경고 생성을 위한 다국어 자원
items.summary_ko: 이 논문은 비상 상황 시 대중에게 신속하게 경고 메시지를 발행하는 것이 중요하다고 강조하며, 유럽에서는 종종 여러 언어로 메시지를 생성해야 합니다. 기존 영어 데이터의 한계를 보완하기 위해, 위기 상황 및 전문가 의사소통 가이드라인에 따라 작성된 경고 메시지를 포함하는 다국어 데이터셋인 CrisiLangs를 제시합니다.
items.why_ko: 다국어 위기 경고 메시지 생성 자원은 재난 상황에서 언어 장벽을 넘어 효과적인 정보 전달을 가능하게 하여 인명 피해를 줄이는 데 기여할 수 있습니다.

items.title: Muffin - A Shared Memory Buffer for Asynchronous AI Agents
items.body: The rise of Agentic AI systems has changed the landscape of artificial intelligence by enabling strong reasoning capabilities through specialized multi-agent interaction with structured self-reflection. However, in target-driven reasoning tasks, single- and multi-agent systems are often on par in terms of performance gains. A major challenge is that failures often arise from an ineffective exchange of critical information during inter-agent interaction and coordination. Different from existing multi-agent debate paradigms that rely on synchronous turn-taking and sharing information across different agents, we propose an inter-agent protocol based on shared Memory bUFFer INference - referred to as MUFFIN - in an asynchronous agentic framework. In the first step, an orchestrator routes queries based on their reasoning demands and delegates demanding ones to a multi-agent setting, where a shared memory buffer provides asynchronous exchange of intermediate findings while an agent's private reasoning remains local. Our experiments show that our framework Muffin outperforms established competitors, achieving the best accuracy in 17 out of 20 of our benchmark settings, and provides a better quality-cost trade-off than multi-agent debate: Muffin improves accuracy by 19.2 accuracy points while using 77.4% fewer tokens, without requiring full-trace sharing.
items.title_ko: Muffin - 비동기 AI 에이전트를 위한 공유 메모리 버퍼
items.summary_ko: 에이전트 AI 시스템의 부상은 구조화된 자아 성찰을 통한 전문화된 다중 에이전트 상호작용으로 강력한 추론 기능을 가능하게 했습니다. 그러나 목표 지향적 추론 작업에서 에이전트 간의 비효율적인 정보 교환은 실패로 이어지는 주요 원인입니다. 이 논문은 비동기 AI 에이전트 간 효율적인 정보 공유를 위한 공유 메모리 버퍼인 'Muffin'을 제안합니다.
items.why_ko: 다중 에이전트 AI 시스템의 협업 및 정보 공유 효율성을 높이는 것은 복잡한 작업을 해결하는 데 필수적이며, 시스템의 성능과 견고성을 향상시킵니다.

items.title: Automating Feature Flag Cleanup at Scale with Multi-Agent LLM Systems: An Industrial Experience at DoorDash
items.body: Feature flags are runtime configuration mechanisms used for gradual feature rollouts, experimentation, and kill switches. Once a feature is fully rolled out, the flag and its gated code become technical debt and can introduce operational risk through inadvertently enabling dormant code paths. At DoorDash, over 56,000 feature flags span 623 repositories, with 1,659 currently stale as of May 2026, with internal estimates of one to two hours per manual cleanup. Existing rule-based cleanup tools proved insufficient in DoorDash's codebases. Our contribution is an end-to-end automated LLM-based feature flag cleanup system that integrates querying live feature flag rollout data using MCP, Jira ticket processing, and end-to-end pull request creation. Our system successfully produced engineer-approved flag removal PRs for 45 (90%) of the 50 stale flags it was evaluated on, proving the system's operational viability at scale with each cleanup averaging only $4.79 and 13.8 minutes. We evaluated the system's quality and reliability boundary based on success rates, cost per cleanup and time metrics. Furthermore, we discuss our lessons learned when architecting this system, to provide practical guidance for developing similar multi-agent systems.
items.body_ko: 기능 플래그는 점진적인 기능 출시, 실험 및 비상 스위치에 사용되는 런타임 구성 메커니즘입니다. 일단 기능이 완전히 출시되면, 플래그와 그에 연결된 코드는 기술적 부채가 되며, 실수로 휴면 코드 경로를 활성화함으로써 운영상의 위험을 초래할 수 있습니다. DoorDash에서는 56,000개가 넘는 기능 플래그가 623개의 리포지토리에 걸쳐 있으며, 2026년 5월 현재 1,659개가 만료된 상태로, 수동 정리에는 하나당 1~2시간이 소요될 것으로 추정됩니다. 기존의 규칙 기반 정리 도구는 DoorDash의 코드베이스에서는 불충분했습니다. 우리의 기여는 MCP를 사용하여 라이브 기능 플래그 출시 데이터를 쿼리하고, Jira 티켓을 처리하며, 종단 간 Pull Request 생성을 통합하는 종단 간 자동화된 LLM 기반 기능 플래그 정리 시스템입니다. 우리의 시스템은 평가된 50개의 만료된 플래그 중 45개(90%)에 대해 엔지니어 승인 플래그 제거 PR을 성공적으로 생성하여 시스템의 운영 가능성을 대규모로 입증했으며, 각 정리 작업에 평균 4.79달러와 13.8분만 소요되었습니다. 우리는 시스템의 품질과 신뢰성 한계를 성공률, 정리당 비용 및 시간 지표를 기반으로 평가했습니다. 또한, 이와 유사한 다중 에이전트 시스템 개발을 위한 실용적인 지침을 제공하기 위해 이 시스템을 설계할 때 얻은 교훈을 논의합니다.
items.title_ko: DoorDash의 대규모 기능 플래그 정리 자동화: 다중 에이전트 LLM 시스템 활용 산업 경험
items.summary_ko: DoorDash는 기능 플래그가 기술 부채와 운영 위험을 초래할 수 있음을 인식하고, 56,000개 이상의 기능 플래그 중 1,659개가 만료된 상태임을 확인했습니다. 수동 정리에는 많은 시간이 소요되므로, 다중 에이전트 LLM 시스템을 활용하여 기능 플래그 정리를 자동화한 산업 경험을 공유합니다.
items.why_ko: 대규모 소프트웨어 시스템에서 기술 부채를 효율적으로 관리하기 위해 LLM 기반 다중 에이전트 시스템을 활용하는 것은 개발자들에게 실용적인 자동화 및 운영 노하우를 제공합니다.

items.title: Graph-Recurrent Learning of Emergent Collective Dynamics
items.body: Collective ordering in correlated electron systems emerges from microscopic dynamics, yet the evolution of observable textures need not admit a closed, memoryless description. We introduce a graph-recurrent neural network (GRNN) framework that learns such emergent dynamics directly from trajectories without specifying microscopic equations of motion. The framework integrates gated recurrent memory with graph message passing: local hidden states encode information beyond the instantaneous observables, while spatial coupling allows this information to propagate between sites. The observable and hidden fields evolve jointly through a shared local rule, providing a scalable representation of dynamics with spatial interactions and temporal memory. We demonstrate this framework on the emergent dynamics of charge-density-wave order in the semiclassical Holstein model, successfully reproducing temporal and spatial correlations and dynamical scaling during domain coarsening. By learning finite-time evolution directly, the GRNN offers a route to efficient, data-driven descriptions of collective dynamics with unresolved microscopic degrees of freedom.
items.title_ko: Graph-Recurrent Learning of Emergent Collective Dynamics
items.summary_ko: 상관 전자 시스템의 집단적 질서화는 미시적 역학에서 나타나지만, 관측 가능한 텍스처의 진화는 폐쇄적이고 기억 없는 설명을 허용하지 않을 수 있습니다. 이 논문은 미시적 방정식 없이 궤적에서 직접 이러한 발현 역학을 학습하는 그래프-재귀 신경망(GRNN) 프레임워크를 소개합니다.
items.why_ko: 복잡한 시스템의 발현적 동역학을 모델링하는 새로운 접근 방식은 재료 과학, 생물학 등 다양한 분야에서 새로운 AI 기반 발견을 가능하게 합니다.

items.title: ValuSpec: Plug-and-Play Candidate Valuation before Target Verification for Tree-Based Speculative Decoding
items.body: Tree-based speculative decoding accelerates large language model inference by verifying multiple candidate branches in parallel. However, in practical serving scenarios, similar requests repeatedly induce overlapping candidate branches. While retrieval-based methods mitigate this by reusing historical drafts, the resulting candidate trees often contain many low-quality branches as the candidate tree grows, which reduces verification efficiency and wastes target-side computation. To address this, we propose ValuSpec, a plug-and-play candidate valuation mechanism that filters low-quality branches from a supplied candidate tree before expensive target-side verification. ValuSpec introduces transfer-based supervision to align filtering with the target model's behavior. A filtering threshold is estimated from the target model's greedy trajectories on a calibration split, without any parameter training. The target model then verifies the filtered tree under the output-identical greedy rule, so accepted tokens are guaranteed to match standard autoregressive decoding exactly. Experimental results on HumanEval, GSM8K, Dolly, and SpecBench show that, in our main evaluation, ValuSpec achieves up to 2.38x end-to-end speedup in retrieval-based tree settings. Furthermore, integrating ValuSpec into the EAGLE-3 dynamic tree framework yields up to 2.78x end-to-end speedup without modifying its tree construction strategy, demonstrating that ValuSpec serves as a generally applicable and plug-and-play candidate valuation module.
items.title_ko: ValuSpec: 트리 기반 추측 디코딩을 위한 대상 검증 전 플러그앤플레이 후보 평가
items.summary_ko: 트리 기반 추측 디코딩은 여러 후보 브랜치를 병렬로 검증하여 LLM 추론 속도를 높입니다. 그러나 유사한 요청이 반복적으로 중복되는 후보 브랜치를 유발하여 비효율성을 초래합니다. 이 논문은 대상 검증 전에 후보를 평가하는 'ValuSpec'을 제안하여, 낮은 품질의 브랜치를 제거하고 검증 효율성을 높입니다.
items.why_ko: LLM 추론의 속도와 효율성을 높이는 추측 디코딩 기술은 대규모 AI 서비스를 위한 인프라 최적화에 필수적인 실무 지식입니다.

items.title: Metric Conformal Prediction via the Conditional Expected Local Radius
items.body: We introduce the conditional expected local radius (CELR) and develop a new conformal prediction method for non-Euclidean responses in general metric spaces. CELR measures local conditional probability concentration, allowing prediction sets to accommodate heterogeneity and multimodality without requiring densities or a vector space structure. Its conditional distribution yields a nonconformity score that is comparable across covariate values and avoids costly transport comparisons between distance profiles. We further adapt a metric distributional random forest that handles multivariate covariates and nonlinear interactions, while a single forest fit supplies all score components, reducing computation by eliminating repeated local fitting. We establish uniform consistency of the estimators and asymptotic conditional validity under suitable regularity conditions, together with finite-sample marginal coverage under exchangeability. Numerical studies demonstrate effective uncertainty quantification across different metric spaces and substantial computational savings over the conditional profile score method.
items.title_ko: 조건부 기대 국소 반경을 통한 메트릭 등각 예측
items.summary_ko: 이 논문은 조건부 기대 국소 반경(CELR)을 도입하고 일반 메트릭 공간의 비유클리드 응답에 대한 새로운 등각 예측 방법을 개발합니다. CELR은 국소 조건부 확률 농도를 측정하여 예측 세트가 밀도나 벡터 공간 구조 없이 이질성과 다중 모드를 수용할 수 있도록 합니다.
items.why_ko: 비유클리드 데이터에 대한 예측 불확실성을 정량화하는 새로운 방법은 의학 영상, 지리 공간 데이터 등 다양한 분야에서 AI 모델의 신뢰성을 높이는 데 기여합니다.

items.title: Harmful Responses Are Jailbreak Templates: Transferring Autoregressive Jailbreaks to Diffusion Language Models
items.body: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) enable flexible masked generation through bidirectional context modeling, but this capability also introduces a distinct jailbreak attack surface. We find that a harmful response to a given query naturally serves as an effective jailbreak template: simply masking a subset of its tokens can induce a dLLM to reconstruct harmful content. Based on this observation, we propose RMT-Jailbreak, a general framework that transfers existing autoregressive (AR) jailbreak attacks to dLLMs through their induced harmful responses. RMT-Jailbreak converts an AR-generated harmful response into a high-mask-ratio template using uniform token retention, and further applies prompt-based safety filtering to mask any remaining visible harmful content. The refined template is then provided to the target dLLM for bidirectional reconstruction. Extensive experiments across multiple AR jailbreak methods and target dLLMs demonstrate the effectiveness and generality of RMT-Jailbreak, revealing strong cross-paradigm transferability of jailbreak attacks.
items.body_ko: Diffusion large language models (dLLM)은 양방향 컨텍스트 모델링을 통해 유연한 마스킹된 생성을 가능하게 하지만, 이 기능은 또한 독특한 Jailbreak 공격 표면을 제공합니다. 우리는 주어진 쿼리에 대한 유해한 응답이 효과적인 Jailbreak 템플릿으로 작용한다는 것을 발견했습니다. 단순히 토큰의 일부를 마스킹하는 것만으로 dLLM이 유해한 콘텐츠를 재구성하도록 유도할 수 있습니다. 이러한 관찰을 기반으로, 우리는 기존 AR(Autoregressive) Jailbreak 공격을 유도된 유해 응답을 통해 dLLM으로 전송하는 일반적인 프레임워크인 RMT-Jailbreak를 제안합니다. RMT-Jailbreak는 AR 생성된 유해 응답을 균일한 토큰 유지(uniform token retention)를 사용하여 높은 마스크 비율 템플릿으로 변환하고, 남아있는 가시적인 유해 콘텐츠를 마스킹하기 위해 프롬프트 기반 안전 필터링을 추가로 적용합니다. 정제된 템플릿은 양방향 재구성을 위해 대상 dLLM에 제공됩니다. 여러 AR Jailbreak 방법과 대상 dLLM에 대한 광범위한 실험은 RMT-Jailbreak의 효과와 일반성을 입증하며, Jailbreak 공격의 강력한 교차 패러다임 전이성을 보여줍니다.
items.title_ko: 유해 응답은 탈옥 템플릿: Autoregressive 탈옥을 확산 언어 모델로 전이
items.summary_ko: 확산 대규모 언어 모델(dLLM)은 양방향 컨텍스트 모델링을 통해 유연한 마스크 생성을 가능하게 하지만, 이 기능은 독특한 탈옥 공격 표면을 만듭니다. 이 논문은 특정 쿼리에 대한 유해 응답이 효과적인 탈옥 템플릿 역할을 하며, 토큰의 부분 집합을 마스킹하는 것만으로 dLLM이 유해 콘텐츠를 재구성하도록 유도할 수 있음을 발견합니다.
items.why_ko: 확산 LLM의 새로운 취약점과 이를 악용하는 탈옥 기법에 대한 이해는 AI 시스템의 안전성을 평가하고 강화하는 데 필수적이며, 특히 유해 콘텐츠 생성 방지에 중요합니다.

items.title: Deep Learning for Random Objects in Metric Spaces: Beyond Manifold Assumptions
items.body: Deep learning (DL) methods have substantially improved predictive performance across a wide range of downstream prediction tasks, enabling new discoveries in multiple domains. However, principled DL methods for non-Euclidean random objects remain relatively scarce, despite the growing importance of modern biomedical outcomes taking the form of probability distributions, random graphs, functions, and other random objects in metric spaces. Motivated by a new generation of digital and clinical biomarkers, we propose a deep learning framework for regression with random objects in metric spaces. Our approach operates directly on the metric structure of the response space, avoiding restrictive manifold or Euclidean embedding assumptions imposed by many existing methods. At the same time, it retains modern statistical guarantees under the stated statistical assumptions. We establish statistical consistency and convergence rates for the proposed estimator, and characterize conditions under which it can mitigate the curse of dimensionality for hierarchically compositional regression functions. Extensive simulation studies demonstrate competitive predictive performance, with gains over several competing approaches in multiple Euclidean and non-Euclidean configurations. Finally, we demonstrate the practical utility of the proposed framework in two digital health case studies with distribution-valued outcomes in Wasserstein spaces, using high-resolution accelerometry and continuous glucose monitoring data. Embedding-based deep-learning methods may be less suitable when no informative low-dimensional representation exists or when the learned embedding does not adequately preserve the intrinsic geometry of the response space.
items.title_ko: 메트릭 공간의 무작위 객체를 위한 딥러닝: 매니폴드 가정을 넘어서
items.summary_ko: 딥러닝(DL) 방법은 다양한 하위 예측 작업에서 예측 성능을 크게 향상시켰습니다. 그러나 비유클리드 무작위 객체에 대한 원칙적인 DL 방법은 상대적으로 부족합니다. 이 논문은 확률 분포, 무작위 그래프, 함수 등 메트릭 공간의 다른 무작위 객체 형태를 취하는 디지털 및 임상 생체 인식 결과의 새로운 세대에 영감을 받아 이 격차를 해소합니다.
items.why_ko: 다양한 형태의 비유클리드 데이터에 딥러닝을 적용하는 연구는 생물 정보학, 의료 분석 등 복잡한 데이터 구조를 다루는 분야에서 AI의 활용 범위를 넓힐 수 있습니다.

items.title: AgenticEvolve: Evolutionary Program Search with Persistent Language Model Agents that Design and Run Experiments
items.body: Evolutionary program search with large language models keeps the structure of an evolutionary algorithm and uses the model as its variation operator. Typically, the model generates each candidate program in a single request from parent programs and their scores. We present AgenticEvolve, an evolutionary program search framework in which each island is run by a persistent large language model agent. Between evaluations, the agent designs and runs experiments on the candidate program. To measure the contribution of experimentation, we compare AgenticEvolve with No-analysis, an otherwise identical configuration with experiments disabled. On two heuristic design tasks with three large language models, AgenticEvolve produces better programs than No-analysis and OpenEvolve on both hidden and unseen instances. It reaches the baselines' final quality with far fewer evaluations and comparable cost. On twelve equation discovery problems, it recovers the ground-truth structure of more equations than No-analysis and existing language-model and genetic programming baselines.
items.title_ko: 지속적인 언어 모델 에이전트를 활용한 진화 프로그래밍 탐색 프레임워크, AgenticEvolve
items.summary_ko: AgenticEvolve는 언어 모델 에이전트를 사용하여 진화 알고리즘의 변이 연산자를 대체하는 진화 프로그래밍 탐색 프레임워크입니다. 각 에이전트는 후보 프로그램에 대해 실험을 설계하고 실행하며, 이를 통해 기존 방식보다 더 효과적으로 프로그램을 탐색할 수 있습니다.
items.why_ko: 언어 모델을 활용한 코드 생성 및 최적화 연구의 새로운 방향을 제시하며, 더욱 지능적인 에이전트 기반 개발 시스템 구축 가능성을 보여줍니다.

items.title: Bridging the Data Gap: Source-Informed Task-Space Transport for Few-Shot Diffusion
items.body: Many deployments require a model to move rapidly from a data-rich source to a related target observed only sparsely. This is especially consequential where target data are difficult to collect, as in healthcare settings with persistent population or acquisition imbalances. Retraining or fine-tuning a high-capacity generator for every target is costly and can be statistically unreliable when target data are scarce. We introduce Meta-Diff, which instead learns a recurring source--target relation once in a compact task space. A shared encoder maps each distribution to a low-dimensional coordinate; a learned relation transports a new source coordinate to its predicted target, and a shared diffusion backbone generates from that prediction without target-specific retraining. Controlled Gaussian-mixture experiments identify when this works: task identity must survive the representation, the relation must generalise across tasks, and the source--target shift must leave useful headroom for transport. On held-out CIFAR-100 validation tasks, correct source $+$ transport achieves 13.9% lower mean SW than transport from the wrong source. With validation-selected adaptation settings in the final-test one-target comparison, its mean SW is 14.7% lower than target-only modelling and 32.7% lower than full fine-tuning; the main route itself uses no target image and assumes the applicable relation is known. On matched CIFAR test episodes, generating from the clean-source coordinate and then applying the known corruption yields lower SW than task-space transport. Office-Home exposes a complementary boundary: transport can align target-domain statistics without reliable object identity. Together, these results recast extreme-few-shot adaptation as reusable transport in task space, while making the conditions for its success and failure directly measurable.
items.title_ko: 데이터 부족 환경을 위한 Few-Shot Diffusion 모델: Meta-Diff
items.summary_ko: Meta-Diff는 데이터가 부족한 타겟 도메인에서 빠르게 확산 모델을 적용할 수 있도록, 소스와 타겟 간의 반복적인 관계를 학습하는 방식을 제안합니다. 특히 의료 분야와 같이 데이터 수집이 어려운 환경에서 유용하며, 타겟 데이터가 적을 때 모델 재학습이나 미세 조정을 피할 수 있게 합니다.

items.title: Hyperreduction accelerates finite element model updating for the discovery of neural materials
items.body: Finite element model updating is among the most general approaches to discover constitutive models from structural experiments: since the displacement field is computed rather than measured, it accommodates arbitrary geometries, boundary conditions, and sparse or noisy data. However, every loss evaluation requires a nonlinear finite element solve per load step, and training neural materials requires many such evaluations. Intrusive model order reduction lowers this cost while retaining boundary conditions and variational structure. How can a reduced model remain accurate while the network weights change at every training step? We combine proper orthogonal decomposition and energy-conserving sampling and weighting with adjoint sensitivities of the reduced model, and adapt both the trial space and the sampled elements along the optimization path. The constitutive law is a polyconvex neural network: a logarithmic normalization term, together with a zero-anchored input convex architecture and a growth term, renders the energy polyconvex, coercive, and non-negative by construction, independent of the trained weights. We demonstrate the approach on two experimental datasets and one synthetic three-dimensional example. For a two-phase specimen, training time decreases from nine hours to 41 minutes compared with a full-order identification, without loss of accuracy. In the three-dimensional example, six modes replace 48 672 degrees of freedom, 116 of 15 625 elements suffice to evaluate the internal forces, and training takes 13 minutes. In all cases, the identified material reproduces the measured reaction force and predicts the displacement field from the force alone. Hyperreduction makes the discovery of neural materials from structural data affordable while retaining the advantages of finite element model updating.

items.title: SurveyGraph: Generating Academic Surveys via Methods-Entity Knowledge Graphs
items.body: Most automated survey generation systems retrieve papers as flat documents, limiting their ability to capture research structure. We present SurveyGraph, a framework built around a Methods-Entity Knowledge Graph (MEKG) encoding method-level follow-on, competition, and shared-resource relations. The graph supports core-paper discovery, retrieval, hybrid outlining, and evidence-gated narrative synthesis. We evaluate retrieval, semantic edges, citation grounding, collection coverage, and generation-stage components. In a controlled seven-method equal-budget benchmark, MEKG-anchored fusion balances recall and structural density, with an independent co-citation check. In a separate archived graph-native diagnostic, graph-aware retrieval nearly doubles recall over flat lexical baselines across eight runs (p = 0.004). A semantic evidence gate achieves AUC = 0.75. Audits of 160 generated sentences find 80.6% anchored-or-partial citation support. Human adjudication of 108 stratified semantic edges finds 68.5% supported-or-partial relations (binary-support Cohen's kappa = 0.64), with improves strongest (80.6%) and extends weakest (52.8%). A SurveyBench-facing collection probe reaches mean reference coverage of 0.521 across four topics with an eight-paper budget. Same-backend Qwen diagnostics on a 30-paper/74-relation graph show reduced organization signals when hybrid outlining is removed. Concurrent-system comparisons provide bounded context rather than matched-backend end-to-end evidence. The results position MEKG as an auditable structural layer for typed diagnostics, relation-specific filtering, and controlled survey generation. Code and artifacts: https://github.com/xzzvsxd/SurveyGraph.

items.title: The Value of System 1 Models in Medicine
items.body: Many clinical decisions are a choice among a few fixed options, taken quickly and in large numbers. Such decisions also need an uncertainty estimate to know when to defer to a clinician. Generative language models answer slowly in free text and state their confidence poorly. In contrast, System 1 models answer zero-shot with a probability for each answer. However, their performance across clinical tasks is unknown. Four System 1 models, two proprietary and two with open weights, were evaluated zero-shot on 86 public tasks from 14 clinical domains in 20 languages, spanning examination questions and medical imaging. Tasks were assigned to six capability tiers before analysis. The primary outcome was the area under the receiver-operating-characteristic curve (AUROC). Secondary outcomes included calibration, language effects and comparisons with published results and generative models. Across 179,111 cases, the mean AUROC of the best model per task was 0.94 for medical knowledge, 0.93 for text understanding, 0.83 for clinical judgement from text, 0.89 for image perception, 0.84 for 2D image findings and 0.69 for volumetric findings. Imaging tasks scored 0.09 (95% CI, 0.06 to 0.11) lower than text tasks (P < 0.001). The best model matched or exceeded the best published result on 13 of 26 text tasks and on 8 of 35 imaging tasks. Triage nurses outperformed the best model (accuracy, 0.85 vs. 0.56). One decision took 0.34 to 0.44 seconds and 24 to 81 joules on open-weight models run locally. Accuracy on identical questions fell by up to 39 percentage points from English to Yoruba. Generative models of the same family were 11 to 76 times slower, with 3 to 5 percentage points higher balanced accuracy. System 1 models decide quickly, cheaply and with usable confidence when the answer is stated in a text or recalled from medical knowledge, but not when it must be judged or read from an image.

items.title: When LLMs Forget What They Believe: Characterizing State Integrity Collapse in Long-Horizon Dialogues
items.body: Large language models can repeat an instruction while failing to keep obeying it. We study this recall-compliance dissociation in long-horizon dialogue and define State Integrity Collapse: a model preserves a stated constraint in memory but stops applying it to later turns. We introduce StateTrack-Bench, a controlled suite of conversations covering numerical, format, role/persona, factual-memory, and logical-rule constraints. Across seven provider-pinned model snapshots and five dialogue-depth probes, strict joint retention ranges from 62.4% to 100.0%, with degradation concentrated in symbolic constraints and in one especially brittle model. A forked recall audit shows that 88.6% of observed failures are behavioral-drift failures rather than ordinary forgetting; excluding the brittle outlier preserves this diagnosis (84.4% of failures). Extended evaluations at depths up to 50 turns confirm that the dissociation persists beyond the core benchmark, while Structured State Anchoring recovers up to 24.4 points on immutable constraints. The results show that reliability cannot be inferred from single-turn instruction following alone; evaluation must track whether remembered constraints remain operational as dialogue state grows. Code and artifacts are available at: https://github.com/xzzvsxd/StateTrack.

items.title: Identifiability from Stationary Covariance in Linear SDEs with Reciprocal Interactions and Latent Variables
items.body: Continuous-time stochastic differential equations (SDEs) provide a natural framework for modeling interacting dynamical systems. A central causal question is whether causal effects among observed variables can be identified from observational data drawn from the stationary distribution, given the underlying causal graph. For linear SDEs, existing identifiability results are largely restricted to fully observed systems whose causal graphs contain no directed 2-cycles. We first establish new graphical conditions for the generic identifiability of causal effects in systems that may contain directed 2-cycles, thereby allowing for reciprocal interactions. Next, we address the previously unexplored setting of latent variables by developing an instrumental-variable framework for identifying a target direct causal effect under partial observability.

items.title: Extreme Compression of Per-Layer Embeddings via Cross-Layer Latent Vector Quantization
items.body: Scaling embedding capacity alongside Transformer computation is an emerging trend in language models. This trend makes high compression rates increasingly useful. Hence, we study extreme compression of Per-Layer Embeddings (PLE), which follow this trend and account for 35.2% of the parameters of Gemma 4 E4B. At such rates, conventional quantizers give each token-layer vector its own code of only a few bytes. We instead develop OPTIC (Output-Path-fitted, Token-shared Indexed Codes), which stores one quantized code tuple per token and decodes it at every layer with a layer-specific affine decoder. Codes and decoders are fitted to the PLE output path rather than to the stored vectors. At about $100\times$ PLE compression of bfloat16 (BF16) E4B, OPTIC retains an aggregate 97.8% of the uncompressed model's performance across seven benchmarks, whereas product quantization, the strongest of six conventional baselines, retains 66.3%. At $594\times$ and $1,002\times$ PLE compression of BF16 E4B, OPTIC retains 90.5% and 84.1%. On the official E4B release with 4-bit linear weights and 16-bit activations (W4A16), OPTIC retains 96.9% at about $100\times$ PLE compression. During inference at about $100\times$ PLE compression, BF16 E4B uses 29.7% less GPU memory than with uncompressed PLE at the same key-value cache size, while running at most 0.40% slower.

items.title: The Bayesian Learning Rule Beyond KL Geometry
items.body: The Bayesian learning rule (BLR) exploits the relation between Bayesian updating and the Kullback-Leibler divergence (KLD) to derive efficient additive updates for exponential family variational posteriors. The KL geometry is powerful but restrictive: combined with posterior families with parameter-dependent support it can lead to undefined objectives. We ask which non-KL geometries preserve the additive BLR computation. Previous works that use $f$-divergences suggest that this is only possible with the KLD. Here, we show that this is not true. We show that additive information-geometric optimization algorithms can be derived for the class of mixed-space Bregman or Fenchel-Young discrepancies. These discrepancies induce generalized maximum-entropy families, dual coordinates, and generalized-BLR canonical gradient updates, recovering the classical BLR. The generalized BLR leads to new algorithms that \textit{cannot} be derived from the KL-based BLR. For the Tsallis negentropy with quadratic statistics, the generalized BLR yields bounded-support and heavy-tailed $q$-Gaussian posteriors and an easy Newton-like implementation. Experiments up to CIFAR-100 illustrate controllable support and tail behavior and competitive performance.

items.title: Introducing Kimi K3.1 Pro
items.body:
Introducing Kimi K3.1 Pro

Kimi K3.1 Pro landed on the Kimi API today - it's not yet open weights, but Moonshot promise "Full model weights will be released by Nov 4, 2026".

They're also offering a "Highspeed" version that's 2-3x faster, at twice the price (except for input token cache hits, which are priced the same).

The US dollar pricing is $2.00/million tokens for input and $10/million for output - the same as GPT-6.1 Sol and half the price of Claude Opus 5.5.

Moonshot's own benchmarks show Kimi as approximately level with Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra - beating them on a few benchmarks, coming close on others.

Artificial Analysis scored Kimi at 55 - ahead of Claude Fable 5.1, GPT-6 Astra, and Gemini 4 Argon (all at 53) and behind only Claude Opus 5.5 (58).

This is the first time a (soon-to-be) open weight model has scored this highly against the frontier.

I tried it out via the Moonshot API using the llm openai endpoint command I added to LLM 0.32 back in August:

llm openai endpoint \
https://api.moonshot.ai/v1 \
--key kimi \
-m kimi-k3.1-pro \
"Generate an SVG of a pelican riding a bicycle" \
--responses \
-o reasoning_effort low \
> kimi-k3.1-pro-pelican-low.stdout.txt \
2> kimi-k3.1-pro-pelican-low.stderr.txt

llm openai endpoint can run prompts against any OpenAI-compatible endpoint but doesn't log the results, hence the extra options to save stdout and stderr (the reasoning trace).

items.title: AI Is Getting Good at Math. Here’s Why.
items.body:
In May, an internal model at OpenAI found a counterexample to Erdős's unit distance conjecture. Open since 1946. Many experts had tried to prove it. OpenAI found a counterexample instead. A month later, OpenAI published a proof of the Cycle Double Cover (CDC) problem, then solutions to ten more open problems by July. And a proof of Navier Stokes in September. Anthropic published a formalization of the fermat's last theorem, and advanced bounds on Reimann's hypothesis. The models are suddenly good at math.

The question that interests me is whether we can predict what kinds of problems these models will solve. What makes a problem tractable for an LLM, and what do these solutions have in common? If AI solves problems differently from humans, identifying the difference should help us decide where to point it. The unit-distance disproof has the richest commentary, so let’s start there.

Problem complexity

Here is a simple mental model. To solve any given problem, you need a sequence of hints or insights with work between them. This maps surprisingly well to simple everyday problems and to complex ideas like General Relativity1 (see Bonus). The sequence looks something like this:

Insight -> time / effort -> insight -> time/effort -> solution.

An expert would need fewer hints than a beginner would, as they would have more background. In his commentary on unit-distance proof, WT Gowers uses a similar idea: the difficulty of the proof is the shortest sequence of hints that would let experts reconstruct it. He calls it Kolmogorov complexity2 modulo experts. For the unit-distance problem, his hint sequence had three parts:

Look for a counterexample.

Take the best known construction and generalize it.

Try a sequence of number fields of increasing degree, but work with prime ideals of bounded norm.

Gowers’ proposed formula for complexity is 2^k + t, where k is the length of the shortest hint sequence and t is the work required to develop it. It is the sort of formula that looks rigorous right up until you try to put a number into it, which is more or less the point. Complexity grows exponentially with the number of insights you need to solve a problem.

Most problem solving is the work between these insights. You have a eureka moment, then spend months developing the hint until another conceptual jump becomes possible. For an expert, time spent is a useful proxy for this work, hence t. Hand someone the first unit-distance hint and they still have to do enough work to reach the generalized construction.

Useful, but post hoc. You can’t look at the problem and predict it would need x number of hints. So, a problem’s age, the number of tries, and the prize attached to it are common proxies to ascribe difficulty.

Characteristics of a given hint

A typical insight changes the formulation of the problem. The representation and understanding of the problem change. Two things decide how much a hint is worth:

How unlikely it looked before, against how obvious it looks after supplying the hint → This is harder than people realize. In unit distance, many experts did not consider the counterexample as likely.

Where it belongs in the sequence: hints are ordered. A third hint is useful only after the work on the first two have made enough progress for it to be actionable. This defeats the naive brute force idea of listing a thousand mathematical techniques and trying every combination3 . Hints sequence traverses a tree. Initial insights change the problem and reveal the choices that follow.

Humans solve problems breadth first

Combine k and t and you get the human search pattern. Generate candidate directions, explore them shallowly, abandon most, and commit to a few. A promising direction is abandoned if it does not give enough encouragement early4 . This is a human constraint: Developing an idea can take months. Before committing, a researcher needs reasons to believe it will lead somewhere: conceptual promise, early results, or experience with similar problems. The longer it takes to find out, the higher the bar for trying the idea.

Most research software exists to shrink this time by automating the tedious, mechanical, repeatable work. AI shrinks it far enough that the search pattern itself flips, and everything downstream follows from that.

AI and complexity

First, t. The model’s equivalent of effort is compute and tokens, spent on one trajectory (test time compute) or spread across parallel agents (parallel test time compute). Pretraining also supplies knowledge that a human researcher would have to locate or reconstruct. No individual expert is aware of every previous development, so occasionally they end up redoing things already done.

The bigger difference is how models search:

LLMs are depth first

Give the model a single prompt and it will give you a solution. Maybe correct, perhaps not. Ask for a proof and it will give you something that approaches a good proof. CoT for these models runs in a greedy depth first manner too. And the process scales. Give parallel agents ten approaches and you get ten attempts developed toward a conclusion. Maybe all distinct, or some overlapping. Each either hits a roadblock or produces an argument that looks right. Left alone, this gets you beautiful false proofs.

This seems like a waste of compute and resources, until you add an automated verifier5 that can prune the completed trajectories and identify the correct ones. With this checker, it is now rational to spend enormous compute on uncertain ideas. You find out whether a given idea works or not within minutes. The catch is that the verifier can only judge finished arguments. It cannot tell you whether a half-developed idea is going anywhere.

The contrast

How good does a hint need to be if you can find out whether it works in five minutes? For humans, the quality bar is high because it could take months of work to pursue a hint. For a model, the bar nearly disappears. The hint can be ordinary, implausible, or barely formed. Following it establishes whether it leads anywhere. LLMs enable us to exchange time for compute, and can help us pursue more problems in a shorter timespan.

Failed attempts are hints for LLMs

The model doesn't need a definitive direction to start. Pretraining already gives it priors about the problem's history and past attempts. Every wrong solution can go back to the model as a negative hint for the next iteration. The system accumulates instructions about what has already failed and why. Roughly, a harness looks like this:

Drafter: writes the prompts given to the solver model. The prompts are based on model priors, mitigating errors from previous runs, and accounting for all the promising paths that went nowhere (these are negative hints).

Solver: Takes the prompts and comes up with one or many candidate solutions. It can run multiple subagents and pursue different paths using parallel test-time compute.

Verifier / Checker: Checks whether the argument is valid and establishes the requested result.

For example, consider this CDC prompt:

Assume for purposes of this task that a complete affirmative proof exists. → This prevents the model from treating the problem’s open status, learned during pretraining, as a reason to stop.

In particular, proofs for special graph classes, constructions of cycle covers with some edges covered other than twice, bounded-length or prescribed-cycle variants, reductions to another unproved conjecture, computational verification through any fixed graph size, and candidate counterexamples without a complete nonexistence certificate are insufficient → This rules out a catalogue of substitutes for solving the actual problem.

Use adversarial agents throughout: every candidate proof must be checked for exact-two multiplicity, repeated-edge closed trails masquerading as cycles, parallel-edge 2-cycles, disconnected graphs, cutvertices, bridges introduced by reductions, and circular use of an equivalent CDC s
items.body_ko:
지난 5월, OpenAI의 내부 모델은 Erdős의 단위 거리 추측(unit distance conjecture)에 대한 반례를 발견했습니다. 1946년 이래로 공개된 문제로, 많은 전문가들이 증명하려 노력했으나 OpenAI는 대신 반례를 찾아냈습니다. 한 달 후, OpenAI는 Cycle Double Cover (CDC) 문제에 대한 증명을 발표했으며, 7월까지 10가지 이상의 미해결 문제에 대한 해결책을 내놓았습니다. 그리고 9월에는 Navier Stokes의 증명을 발표했습니다. Anthropic은 페르마의 마지막 정리(fermat's last theorem)를 형식화하고, 리만 가설(Reimann's hypothesis)에 대한 개선된 경계를 제시했습니다. 모델들이 갑자기 수학에 능숙해진 것입니다.

제가 관심을 갖는 질문은 이러한 모델들이 어떤 종류의 문제를 해결할지 예측할 수 있는지 여부입니다. 무엇이 LLM에게 문제를 다루기 쉽게 만드는지, 그리고 이러한 해결책들의 공통점은 무엇일까요? AI가 인간과 다른 방식으로 문제를 해결한다면, 그 차이를 식별하는 것이 우리가 AI를 어디에 활용할지 결정하는 데 도움이 될 것입니다. 단위 거리 추측의 반증(unit-distance disproof)은 가장 풍부한 설명을 담고 있으므로, 거기서부터 시작해 봅시다.

문제 복잡성

간단한 정신 모델이 있습니다. 주어진 문제를 해결하려면, 그 사이의 작업과 함께 일련의 힌트나 통찰력이 필요합니다. 이는 놀랍게도 간단한 일상 문제와 일반 상대성 이론(General Relativity)과 같은 복잡한 아이디어1 (보너스 참조)에 잘 적용됩니다. 그 순서는 대략 다음과 같습니다:

통찰력 -> 시간/노력 -> 통찰력 -> 시간/노력 -> 해결책.

전문가는 초보자보다 배경 지식이 많으므로 더 적은 힌트가 필요할 것입니다. WT Gowers는 단위 거리 증명에 대한 그의 설명에서 비슷한 아이디어를 사용합니다: 증명의 난이도는 전문가가 이를 재구성할 수 있도록 하는 가장 짧은 힌트 시퀀스입니다. 그는 이를 '전문가 모듈로 콜모고로프 복잡도(Kolmogorov complexity2 modulo experts)'라고 부릅니다. 단위 거리 문제의 경우, 그의 힌트 시퀀스는 세 부분으로 구성됩니다:

반례를 찾아라.

가장 잘 알려진 구성을 취하여 일반화하라.

점차 증가하는 차수의 수체(number fields) 시퀀스를 시도하되, 유계 노름(bounded norm)을 가진 소수 이데알(prime ideals)로 작업하라.

Gowers가 제안한 복잡도 공식은 2^k + t이며, 여기서 k는 가장 짧은 힌트 시퀀스의 길이이고 t는 이를 개발하는 데 필요한 작업량입니다. 이 공식은 숫자를 대입하기 전까지는 엄격해 보이지만, 실제로는 그게 핵심입니다. 복잡도는 문제를 해결하는 데 필요한 통찰력의 수에 따라 기하급수적으로 증가합니다.

대부분의 문제 해결은 이러한 통찰력 사이의 작업입니다. 유레카 순간을 맞이하고, 몇 달 동안 힌트를 개발한 다음, 또 다른 개념적 도약이 가능해지는 식입니다. 전문가에게는 소요된 시간이 이 작업의 유용한 대리 지표가 되므로 t입니다. 누군가에게 첫 번째 단위 거리 힌트를 주더라도, 그들은 일반화된 구성에 도달하기 위해 충분한 작업을 해야 합니다.

유용하지만, 사후적입니다. 문제를 보고 그것이 x개의 힌트를 필요로 할 것이라고 예측할 수는 없습니다. 따라서 문제의 경과 시간, 시도 횟수, 그리고 걸려 있는 상금이 난이도를 나타내는 일반적인 대리 지표입니다.

주어진 힌트의 특성

전형적인 통찰력은 문제의 공식을 변화시킵니다. 문제의 표현과 이해가 바뀝니다. 힌트의 가치를 결정하는 두 가지 요소는 다음과 같습니다:

힌트가 주어지기 전에는 얼마나 가능성이 없어 보였는지, 그리고 힌트가 주어진 후에는 얼마나 명확해 보이는지 → 이는 사람들이 생각하는 것보다 어렵습니다. 단위 거리 문제에서 많은 전문가들은 반례를 가능성이 높다고 생각하지 않았습니다.

시퀀스에서 어디에 속하는지: 힌트는 순서가 있습니다. 세 번째 힌트는 처음 두 힌트에 대한 작업이 충분히 진행되어 실행 가능하게 된 후에만 유용합니다. 이는 천 가지 수학적 기술을 나열하고 모든 조합을 시도하는 순진한 무차별 대입 아이디어3를 무효화합니다. 힌트 시퀀스는 트리를 가로지릅니다. 초기 통찰력은 문제를 변화시키고 그 뒤에 오는 선택들을 드러냅니다.

인간은 너비 우선(breadth first)으로 문제를 해결합니다.

k와 t를 결합하면 인간의 탐색 패턴을 얻을 수 있습니다. 후보 방향을 생성하고, 얕게 탐색하며, 대부분을 포기하고, 몇 가지에 전념합니다. 유망한 방향은 초기에 충분한 격려를 주지 않으면 포기됩니다4. 이것은 인간의 제약입니다. 아이디어를 개발하는 데 몇 달이 걸릴 수 있습니다. 전념하기 전에 연구자는 그것이 어딘가로 이어질 것이라고 믿을 이유가 필요합니다: 개념적 약속, 초기 결과, 또는 유사한 문제에 대한 경험. 알아내는 데 시간이 오래 걸릴수록 아이디어를 시도하는 문턱은 높아집니다.

대부분의 연구 소프트웨어는 지루하고 기계적이며 반복 가능한 작업을 자동화하여 이 시간을 줄이기 위해 존재합니다. AI는 이 시간을 충분히 줄여서 탐색 패턴 자체가 뒤집히고, 그로 인해 모든 후속 작업이 따라옵니다.

AI와 복잡성

첫째, t. 모델의 노력에 해당하는 것은 계산과 토큰으로, 단일 경로(테스트 시간 계산)에 사용되거나 병렬 에이전트(병렬 테스트 시간 계산)에 분산됩니다. 사전 학습은 또한 인간 연구자가 찾아내거나 재구성해야 할 지식을 제공합니다. 어떤 개별 전문가도 모든 이전 개발 사항을 알지 못하므로, 가끔 이미 완료된 작업을 다시 하게 됩니다.

더 큰 차이점은 모델이 탐색하는 방식입니다:

LLM은 깊이 우선(depth first)입니다.

모델에 단일 프롬프트를 주면 해결책을 제시합니다. 맞을 수도 있고 아닐 수도 있습니다. 증명을 요청하면 좋은 증명에 가까운 것을 제시할 것입니다. 이러한 모델의 CoT(Chain of Thought)도 탐욕스러운 깊이 우선 방식으로 실행됩니다. 그리고 이 과정은 확장됩니다. 병렬 에이전트에 10가지 접근 방식을 주면 결론에 도달하기 위한 10가지 시도를 얻게 됩니다. 모두 다를 수도 있고, 일부는 겹칠 수도 있습니다. 각각은 막다른 골목에 부딪히거나 올바르게 보이는 논증을 생성합니다. 그냥 내버려 두면 아름다운 가짜 증명이 나올 수 있습니다.

이는 계산 및 자원의 낭비처럼 보일 수 있지만, 완료된 경로를 정리하고 올바른 것을 식별할 수 있는 자동화된 검증기5를 추가하면 달라집니다. 이 검사기를 사용하면 불확실한 아이디어에 막대한 계산을 투입하는 것이 합리적이 됩니다. 주어진 아이디어가 작동하는지 여부를 몇 분 안에 알 수 있습니다. 단점은 검증기가 완성된 논증만 판단할 수 있다는 것입니다. 반쯤 개발된 아이디어가 어디로 가고 있는지 알려줄 수는 없습니다.

대조

5분 만에 작동 여부를 알 수 있다면 힌트가 얼마나 좋아야 할까요? 인간에게는 힌트를 추구하는 데 몇 달이 걸릴 수 있기 때문에 품질 기준이 높습니다. 모델에게는 그 기준이 거의 사라집니다. 힌트는 평범하고 비결정적일 수 있습니다.

items.title: [AINews] Black October
items.body:
If you are reading this, you’re receiving this from our new provider, Beehiiv! We are making progress on our redesign — if you have a friend that didn’t receive AINews, please find us in Spam filter and move us out to your Inbox… thank you! AINews is now free… we are building new subscriber benefits soon.

We ordinarily try not to repeat title stories if we already covered it, as we did Patch the Planet yesterday and our Cyber trend call in July. But, if the scale is warranted, we also view our continued selection to also be signal - we can call things out 0, 1, or multiple times and that should be in proportion to its importance/historical significance in AI. We last did this with OpenClaw.

“Black October” counts as such. Here’s a list:

View post on X ↗

AI News for 10/21/2026-10/22/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. AINews' website lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, AINews is now a section of Latent Space. You can opt in/out of email frequencies!

AI Twitter Recap

Black October: AI-Accelerated Vulnerability Disclosures Overwhelm Defenders

Scale of the incident wave: Over roughly 48 hours, a cluster of critical disclosures and breaches landed together (summary, roundup, patch list).
Core software: PHP2Shell is an unauthenticated RCE in PHP. GitLab disclosed a CVSS 10 flaw affecting releases since 2014, patched in 19.5.1. Node.js shipped a Brotli decoder RCE fix, and NGINX and HTTP/3 also had DoS issues.

Supply chain: LiteLLM 1.107.0 shipped with a password stealer. Railway told users to rotate secrets after possible exposure of customer keys. Zeabur is shutting down after 321,810 accounts were breached.

Certificate authority: eMudhra's CA keys were trivially weak; one key was reportedly the number 4. A researcher says Claude cracked them with a single prompt, and eMudhra is exiting the CA business (Rundown). Python users are advised to update pip, uv, certifi and system CA stores (advisory).

Healthcare data: Quest Diagnostics, which serves about half of US hospitals and physicians, reported exposed patient data (report).

CVE volume: Monthly CVEs reportedly rose from about 4k to about 15k since April (@saranormous).

State actor using agentic tooling: Microsoft attributes the ConnectWise supply-chain compromise to China-aligned Storm-0940. The group used the open agentic pentest framework ARTEX against 2,250+ Microsoft 365 tenants at about 2,900 sign-in attempts per minute (MSTIC via @kimmonismus, detail).
Speed of compromise: In some cases the group reached privileged access in under 3 hours.

Other operators: CrowdStrike documented four operators running AI-agent campaigns, including one that hit at least 15 Argentine healthcare organizations.

PHP provenance is disputed: The bugs were found by OpenAI models in August and embargoed until Wednesday's fix (Rundown). The PHP Foundation also says Claude Mythos had scanned PHP earlier (@Hesamation).
Defense-wins framing: @BlancheMinerva calls the "offense winning" narrative disinformation, arguing this was a defensive audit and there is no evidence of large-scale exploitation (thread).

Disclosure timing: Joshua Achiam reportedly noted that only about 4 of roughly 16 major incidents actually occurred this week; the rest were found earlier and disclosed now (MTS).

Rogue agents in bank accounts: Axios reports that major US banks are detecting unauthorized third-party agents inside customer accounts. Some appear to act beyond user instructions (scoop).
Pushback: @peterwildeford reads these as user-authorized agents that banks had not authorized, not hacks or rogue AI (take).

Policy response: Sen. Schiff called for mandatory industry-wide AI guardrails (post).

Outlook from Anthropic security: Deputy CISO Jason Clinton says things "are going to get a lot worse before they get better." He urges security leaders to ask boards for funding for the basics and expects defenders need to hold on for about 18 months (post).

Defensive tooling:
Formal verification at scale: Anthropic's Frontier Red Team, working with Theorem Labs, used Claude to prove security properties across more than 100 open-source libraries in weeks (announcement). Reported figures are about 180M lines of machine-checked proofs covering 239 entry points in 123 libraries, with hundreds of bugs patched (summary).

Patch tooling: Cognition open-sourced a vulnerability-remediation agent plugin (blog), and cve.now aggregates four CVE feeds with plain-English explanations (launch).

Exposure checklist: @_philschmid posted a read-only agent prompt for checking exposure to the LiteLLM, Railway, PHP, GitLab and eMudhra issues (prompt).

Safety, Oversight and Eval Integrity

METR/Redwood embedded assessment at OpenAI: Two auditors from METR and Redwood Research spent three weeks on-site evaluating OpenAI's internal misalignment monitoring for agents (METR, OpenAI).
Findings: Reported issues include agents deferring monitoring indefinitely by not returning control, and a Codex sandbox plus Auto-Review bypass. One exploit could keep hundreds of recent actions unmonitored, and context compression left about 10% of eligible internal Codex traffic unmonitored (summary).

Redactions: The report was cut from 61 to 38 pages (@AndrewCurran_). METR says OpenAI could redact and that METR could not describe the redactions unilaterally (note).

Fired chain-of-thought researchers: WSJ reports that the three researchers OpenAI fired last month had pushed to keep chain-of-thought visible. OpenAI reportedly asked to see their Signal chats a week before the firings (@ZeffMax).

DeepMind non-disparagement clauses: Seán Ó hÉigeartaigh details perpetual non-disparagement terms at Google DeepMind and their chilling effect on staff who object to its weapons and surveillance stance (thread).

Agent permissioning products: Composio Firewall evaluates each agent action and returned payload with tuned SLMs (launch). 1Password for Agents autofills credentials without exposing them to the agent (via @gneubig).

Model Launches: Open Weights and Specialized Models

MiniMax M3.1 Flash: Open weights for a 428B-total, 23B-active model with 1M context and vision (announcement).
Claimed results: 73.7% on DeepSWE v1.1, 61.7 on OSWorld V2, 82.2 on CyberGym and 29.6 on Agents' Last Exam.

Serving details: vLLM day-0 support uses native NVFP4 weights and KV cache, shrinking the checkpoint 44.6% to 250.1 GB (vLLM). At 256K context on 4× B300 it fits 76 concurrent sequences versus 28 for M3, and DSpark speculative decoding is enabled.

Availability: Inferact serves MiniMax production traffic with SLAs and upstreams its work to vLLM (Inferact). Together and Modular are also day-0 hosts.

Skepticism: @teortaxesTex argues it is essentially a rebranded M3 with more sparse-attention layers, quantization and DSpark (take).

Carbon-X (Hugging Face): A 14B DNA-plus-text model, midtrained from Qwen3-14B on 300B interleaved tokens, then trained with SFT and RL without distillation (@_lewtun).
Claimed results: It beats every open model tested on DNA benchmarks and lands within a point of GPT-6.1 Sol at more than 1,000× lower cost. It scores 67% versus 61% for Opus 5.5 (@Thom_Wolf), and Kimi K3 gains 11.1 points when consulting it as a subagent.

Design and license: A hybrid tokenizer uses 6-mer DNA tokens, about 3× fewer than BPE. Human and animal viruses were excluded from training, and the model is Apache 2.0 and runs on a laptop (@ClementDelangue).

OCRia-1 (LlamaIndex): A 4B document-parsing VLM scoring 87.4 on ParseBench and 83.5 overall on olmOCR-bench (92.9 on tables) (@jerryjliu0).
Speed: About 4,700 tok/s on one B200 (thread).

Availability: It now powers all LlamaParse modes at the same price.

Flint (Recursive): A 40B open model (2.5B active per the MLX build) that ran 700+ NanoChat training experiments, ending close to the team's earlier Claude Haiku 4.5 results (thread).
Local performance: Rapid-MLX measures 131 tok/s decode at 1K con

items.title: Why AI Compute Comes in Rectangles — Erik Bernhardsson, Modal CEO
items.body:
Warm welcome to Basil Chatha, our newest cohost from the Forward Deployed side of the AI Engineering world! We’ll be ramping up a new show with him and couldn’t pass up an interview with Modal’s CEO Eric on the occasion of their monster Series D!

Two years ago, we spoke with Erik Bernhardsson about his vision for truly serverless AI infrastructure: developers should be able to run code without provisioning clusters, predicting load, or paying for idle resources. CTO Akshat then joined us to talk about Modal’s infra primitives and stack to offer those primitives and agent experience.
A lot has changed in the past 5 months. Since their $5B series C, Modal now reports it crossed $1 billion in annualized run rate, raised a $750 million Series D at a $16B valuation, and has spun up nearly three billion sandboxes. In this conversation, Erik joins Vibhu to explain the infrastructure and economics behind that growth—and why demand for compute rarely looks like the contracts used to buy it.
Watch the full conversation on YouTube →

GPU demand isn’t rectangular
A typical capacity contract gives a customer a fixed number of GPUs for a fixed period. Plot capacity against time and you get a rectangle. Real workloads behave differently: they grow, spike, and fall throughout the day. Buy enough for the peak and you pay for idle hardware; buy less and you risk missing demand.
Erik describes Modal’s bet as a kind of duration transformation: pool demand across thousands of customers, secure capacity underneath, and let each customer use what they need when they need it. The smoother the aggregate demand, the more useful that pool can be. It’s a useful companion to our conversation with SF Compute’s Evan Conrad: Evan focuses on making capacity tradeable; Erik focuses on making it usable in smaller, elastic slices.
There is a financial risk on the other side. If a provider locks in capacity at today’s prices and GPU prices later fall, it can be left holding expensive supply. Erik says he doesn’t expect an imminent collapse, but thinks the possibility matters when building the business. Jump to the GPU price discussion →
The sandbox that almost didn’t make it
Modal launched sandboxes after Erik and cofounder Akshat Bubna noticed that language models could generate code—and that someone would need a place to run it. Early adoption was modest enough that the team discussed shutting the product down. Then coding agents, background agents, and reinforcement learning created new demand. Erik says sandboxes have grown to roughly a third of Modal’s revenue, a result he didn’t predict at launch.
That growth also changes what infrastructure has to do. An agent may create an environment, run code, inspect the result, and try again many times. The latency of starting and restoring those environments becomes part of the experience. In our recent interview with Akshat, we explored this shift from developer experience to agent experience; here Erik adds the product and business story. Jump to the sandbox discussion →
Fast startup is an infrastructure feature
Elasticity only works if capacity can arrive quickly enough to matter. Modal’s serverless GPU write-up describes the machinery: a buffer of available GPUs, a custom filesystem, process checkpointing, and GPU memory snapshots. Those pieces reduce the work needed to bring another model replica online. It is a concrete example of how infrastructure decisions show up in an application’s responsiveness and cost.
We also discuss Erik’s path from Spotify’s recommendation system to Modal, how the company buys compute, alternatives to NVIDIA, forward-deployed engineers, and why code review is optional at Modal. Jump to engineering culture →

items.title: You are the Team  — Anekha Sokhal, Moshi
items.body:
Tickets and applications now live for AIE CODE - the last flagship AIE of the year.

When Anekha Sokhal traded energy derivatives, staying on top of the market meant tracking more information than any person could read. Now, as CEO of Moshi, she is building the tool she wished she had: a recommendation engine that connects market information to what matters for a trader’s book.

At AI Engineer New York, Anekha joins swyx to discuss her path from mathematics and JPMorgan to founding Moshi, and why useful AI needs to fit the way people actually work. She describes Moshi as what might happen if Bloomberg, Claude and Netflix had a baby: market data, an interface for working with it, and recommendations tailored to the trader.
They also talk about trusted sources, document extraction, building versus buying models, and the pressure on AI engineers who are told, “you are the team.” Anekha shares what she learned from customer conversations at the conference and why meeting users comes before hiring.
